name: Cairo
baseline: Skia v90 (CPU raster pipeline, built as AVX2 and SSE2 variants, driven through the skia-rs wrapper); tiny-skia and raqote are the other rows in the same suite
workload: cairo image surface (ARGB32, 1000x1000) versus Skia, tiny-skia and raqote in the tiny-skia benchmark suite: single-fill blend modes with two overlapping non-AA paths, rect fills, whole-surface fill, gradients, image patterns, clipping, hairlines and a spiral; time reported in ns per iteration (cargo bench).
claimed_speedup: Mixed result, Cairo wins only some rows. Cairo ns per iteration versus Skia AVX2 / Skia SSE2 / tiny-skia AVX2: Source Over 211,778 vs 253,486 / 515,638 / 366,536; Destination Over 229,726 vs 303,462 / 591,337 / 441,886; Plus 121,081 vs 288,057 / 587,272 / 385,336; Rect fill 204,938 vs 342,526 / 760,673 / 509,752; Rect AA 206,799 vs 365,104 / 777,911 / 554,033; Nearest-neighbour pattern 759,332 vs 1,153,222 / 2,261,130 / 1,940,391. Ratios (derived from page data): Cairo is 1.20x faster than Skia AVX2 on Source Over, 1.32x on Destination Over, 2.38x on Plus, 1.67x on Rect, 1.77x on Rect AA and 1.52x on Nearest, and 2.4x to 4.9x faster than Skia SSE2 on those rows. Cairo is slower on most other rows, for example Source In 1,069,900 vs 290,673 (Skia AVX2), Screen 3,814,683 vs 311,738, bilinear pattern 17,396,620 vs 2,979,746 and AA hairline 13,508,248 vs 1,855,764. The tiny-skia README itself says only that tiny-skia is faster than cairo and raqote 'in many cases'.
compiler_and_flags: cairo v1.16.0 built with gcc -march=native (the Gentoo system build; gcc version and -O level not stated); Skia m90 built with clang 13, -march=haswell for the AVX2 numbers and -march=x86-64 for the SSE2 numbers, with -DSK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER; benchmarks are Rust 1.62 nightly cargo bench using cairo-rs 0.8 bindings (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/linebender/tiny-skia/HEAD/benches/README.md)
hardware: AMD 3700X on Gentoo Linux (x86-64 results page); an Apple M1 ARM page also exists but was not used here
tradeoffs: Dual-licensed LGPL-2.1 or MPL-1.1 C library with a full vector API and PDF, PS, SVG and X11 backends, so it carries more machinery than a pure rasterizer. Its image backend gets its speed from pixman's hand-tuned SIMD fast paths for simple Porter-Duff operators (Over, Add, Over-reverse) and rectangles; the non-separable and separable blend modes, bilinear and high-quality filters, and anti-aliased hairlines go through slow generic paths.
caveats: This is a mixed result in a competitor's suite (the tiny-skia author runs it to show tiny-skia, not Cairo, in the best light). Cairo is slower than Skia AVX2 on most rows, roughly 3.7x on Source In, 12x on Screen, 5x on Hue, 5.8x on bilinear patterns and 7.3x on AA hairlines (derived from page data), and the bicubic row compares cairo's Gaussian 'best' filter with Skia's bicubic. Skia is built with SK_FORCE_RASTER_PIPELINE_BLITTER, which forces its generic raster-pipeline blitter instead of its hand-tuned legacy paths, so the Skia baseline is not Skia at its fastest for simple operators. The Cairo 'Rect' row leaves antialiasing at the cairo default for fractional rectangle coordinates while the tiny-skia row uses anti_alias=false, so it is not like-for-like. Modulate is unsupported in cairo (reported as 0). Cairo 1.16.0 is from 2018 and the run used Rust 1.62 (2022), so the numbers do not reflect Cairo 1.18. The linebender.github.io results page was EGRESS_BLOCKED; the numbers were read from the page's source on the gh-pages branch at the raw.githubusercontent.com URL (same data), and the benchmark code in tiny-skia/benches/src (blend.rs, fill.rs, patterns.rs) was read. The Cairo site and gitlab.freedesktop.org were also EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the repo URL, last commit date and star count could not be opened; the licence comes from a distro package listing in a search result (Cairo 1.18.2). The pixman build used under cairo is not described.
found_via: seed-record pass: awesome-cpp#Graphics and awesome-c#Graphics list ('2D graphics library', http://cairographics.org/); evidence found through https://github.com/RazrFalcon/tiny-skia (README claim that tiny-skia is faster than cairo in many cases), https://raw.githubusercontent.com/linebender/tiny-skia/HEAD/benches/README.md and the gh-pages x86_64.html data

name: CCAN htable (ccan/htable)
baseline: Judy arrays (JudyL, the Judy integer-key sparse array library)
workload: 50,000,000 objects, total time divided by object count to give ns per operation: initial insert, in-order (linear) hit and random hit lookups, with dense sequential keys and then with sparse keys after delete and reinsert; htable run at 75 percent full (dense), 37 percent full (sparse) and 37 percent full with pointer bit-stealing disabled (dumb).
claimed_speedup: htable wins random lookups and loses inserts and in-order lookups. Random hit, dense keys: Judy 361 ns, htable 330 (dense) / 357 (sparse) / 375 (dumb) ns. Random hit, sparse keys: Judy 736 ns, htable 405 / 386 / 445 ns, which is 1.65x to 1.9x faster (derived from page data). Judy wins initial insert (137 ns vs 332 / 471 / 482 ns) and linear hit (19 ns vs 174 / 176 / 214 ns on dense keys; 61 vs 215 / 202 / 265 ns on sparse keys).
stars_or_usage: 1.2k stars (CCAN repo); search results show htable vendored in Samba (lib/ccan) and a 2014 htable licence-change request for Ruby
tradeoffs: Unordered hash table of pointers with user-supplied hash and equality callbacks (htable_type.h adds typed wrappers) and a pointer bit-stealing mode that saves memory; no ordered iteration, unlike Judy, which is sorted and wins on dense in-order access. LGPL-2.1+ licence, C only.
caveats: Snippet only: rusty.ozlabs.org was EGRESS_BLOCKED, so the post was not opened; the numbers come from a web-search result summary of the post and could not be checked against the page, and the machine, CPU, compiler and flags are unknown (hence tier C and confidence 0.45). First-party author blog post from November 2010, on code that has been changed many times since (htable commits through August 2026). The repo's ccan/htable/tools/speed.c, stringspeed.c and hsearchspeed.c time htable alone (the only Judy reference is a comment about in-order lookups being cache-friendly for Judy), so the Judy comparison is not reproducible from the repo; no result numbers are published in the repo. Judy is a strong incumbent but not a standard-library facility, and the win is only on random-access lookups, not on inserts or sequential access. Searches of the CCAN _info files and tools found no other numeric comparison for any CCAN module.
